analysis.title: Global Economics Wrap-Up: November 13, 2026
key_insights: GS expects global GDP growth of 2.8% in 2027, as lower energy prices and strong AI capex outweigh tighter financial conditions and more neutral fiscal policy.

GS sees global risks tilted to the downside: renewed Iran escalation could cause another energy price surge, large fiscal deficits (especially France) could push long-term yields up sharply, and AI capex could disappoint on capacity constraints, regulation, credit stress or weaker demand.

Global inflation should slow in 2027 as the energy impulse fades while lapping the Iran war outbreak, AI-related pressures ease as production capacity rises, and US tariff pass-through ends. GS sees the risks on energy and AI pass-through as to the upside.

GS expects two more Fed hikes and one ECB hike, with both returning to cuts in late 2027. Most of its forecasts for other central banks are below market pricing, and it expects longer-term rates to come down modestly.

GS expects a 25bp Fed hike in December and added a third 25bp hike in March 2027. The October CPI report surprised meaningfully to the upside across several categories and was the third month of worse inflation news.

A third hike could come in January, but GS thinks March is more likely because it expects softer November and December inflation reports, followed by larger start-of-year price increases boosting January inflation.

GS says oil futures have fallen substantially since the elections, so the bulk of the energy-shock pass-through to consumer prices should be behind us. It remains confident inflation will be meaningfully lower by end-2027.
GS suspects the recent inflation prints will lead most FOMC participants to signal a third hike in the December dot plot.
GS left its terminal fed funds forecast unchanged at 3.25-3.5%, but now expects cuts to begin one quarter later, in November 2027, followed by cuts in March, June and September 2028.
GS expects US consumer spending to rise 2.2% in 2027. It estimates 2.5% growth in 2026 on a Q4/Q4 basis, driven by strong Q2 and Q3 as tax refunds and equity gains offset higher energy prices.

GS expects real income growth to pick up to 2.3% in 2027 on disinflation, with household wealth supportive. It sees a softer start to 2027 on higher rates hitting durables, elevated energy prices and lower nonprofit spending after the midterms, then a pickup. Downside risk comes from a fading wealth effect.
GS forecasts 2027 real business fixed investment growth of 8% Q4/Q4, after an 11% annualized pace in 2026Q1-Q3, with another strong quarter expected in Q4.
GS estimates AI-related hardware and IP spending will exceed $900bn annualized by end-2026 (up $550bn from 2025) and reach $1.4tn by end-2027 (up a further $500bn), roughly 4% of US GDP.

The GDP impact of AI capex is smaller than spending data suggest, because semiconductor investment is undercounted in GDP and most information processing equipment is imported. GS estimates AI investment adds 4.3pp to measured capex growth and 0.2pp to GDP growth in 2027.

Midterm election results pose only modest risk to AI investment for now, since data center moratoria likely affect only projects not yet permitted. Declining IRA and CHIPS Act factory spending weighs on capex, partly offset by equipment outfitting. Energy investment should be a positive in 2027 as US oil producers raise capex.
GS forecasts 2027 US real GDP growth of 2.4% on a Q4/Q4 basis.

GS expects euro area growth of 0.9% in 2027, below the recent run rate, potential and consensus. Headwinds are high energy prices slowing consumption over winter, tighter credit, and French stagnation until the elections. Global manufacturing, German fiscal expansion and Southern Europe structural gains cushion them.

Euro area headline inflation should stay near 4% through winter, with core peaking at 2.9% in Q2. GS expects one more ECB hike in December and normalisation cuts from 2027Q4. French budget tensions are the main risk.

UK Q3 real GDP rose 0.7% qoq, in line with expectations. GS expects October inflation of 3.7% yoy, September unemployment edging down a tenth to 4.6%, and private sector regular pay growth ticking up to 3.1%.

China's October trade surplus narrowed to $105.3bn from $133.5bn in September. Export growth was 35.2% yoy (vs 36.3%) and imports surprised up at 41.6% yoy (vs 31%), with energy contributing about 7pp of import growth.
China October headline CPI eased to 0.7% yoy from 0.9% on lower food prices. PPI rose to 5.7% yoy from 5.0% on energy and chemical prices.
EM central banks: Peru hiked 25bp to 4.5% (in line), Romania held at 6.5% (as expected), Mexico cut 25bp to 6.25% in a dovish surprise, and Czechia hiked 25bp to 4% (in line).

French budget tensions and elections: France expected to stagnate until the elections, and large deficits could push long-term yields up sharply.

tension_points.bull_case: GS expects AI hardware and IP spending to reach $1.4tn by end-2027 (about 4% of US GDP), with business fixed investment growing 8% Q4/Q4 and AI the dominant driver.
tension_points.bear_case: AI capex could disappoint because of capacity constraints, regulation, credit market stress or weaker demand. Data center moratoria after the midterms are a modest risk.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Moratoria on data centers extending to already-permitted projects, which would affect planned 2027 construction.

tension_points.bull_case: Inflation falls meaningfully by end-2027 as the energy impulse fades, AI price pressures ease and tariff pass-through ends. Oil futures have fallen substantially since the elections.
tension_points.bear_case: Risks on energy and AI pass-through are to the upside. October CPI was a third month of upside surprises, and larger start-of-year price increases are expected in January.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Renewed Iran escalation causing another energy price surge, or softer November and December inflation reports failing to materialize.
